The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology

Presentation, management, and outcomes of ectopic Cushing syndrome: an international, multicentre, retrospective, cohort study

Chacko SR, Peersen AF, Kaplan JM et al. · 2026 Nov 03
Study Type: International, multicentre, retrospective cohort study (49 tertiary centres, n=1,463).
Key Question: What are the presentation, complications and mortality of ectopic Cushing syndrome, and does early biochemical remission improve outcomes?
Key Findings:
  • 57.1% had metastatic disease; severe hypercortisolism (91.1%) and hypokalaemia (79.4%) were common. Median follow-up was 57 months; 13.4% died from Cushing syndrome-related causes and 42.8% overall. Infection (31.7%) and VTE (8.5%) were the commonest complications.
  • Complete biochemical remission within 6 months was independently associated with fewer late complications (adjusted HR 0.55, 95% CI 0.38–0.80) and lower Cushing syndrome-related mortality (aHR 0.49, 0.27–0.89), with no effect on non-Cushing mortality.
Clinical Relevance: Supports treating ectopic Cushing as a time-critical emergency, favouring early source control or rapid medical/surgical cortisol suppression, with consideration of infection and VTE prophylaxis, in UK specialist and MDT pathways.
Limitations: Retrospective design at high-volume referral centres, with expert-adjudicated diagnosis and investigator-adjudicated outcomes, risks selection bias, immortal-time and confounding by indication (patients achieving remission may have less aggressive tumours), so causality cannot be inferred.

The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism

Clinical and Molecular Predictors of Malignancy in a Series of 585 RAS-positive Thyroid Nodules with Surgical Outcome

Doerfler WR, Argueta AS, Nikitski AV et al. · 2026 Nov 07
Study Type: Single-centre retrospective cohort study (n=585 resected RAS-positive nodules; 55 non-resected), ThyroSeq v3, 2018–2024.
Key Question: Which clinical and molecular features predict malignancy or NIFTP in RAS-positive thyroid nodules, and what are the long-term outcomes?
Key Findings:
  • Of resected nodules, 51% were cancer, 25% NIFTP and 24% benign. Cancer/NIFTP rates differed by RAS subtype: KRAS 34%, NRAS 74%, HRAS 81% (p<0.0001).
  • Independent predictors of cancer/NIFTP: copy number alterations (OR 12, p=0.02), larger ultrasound size (OR 1.3, p=0.003), and Bethesda IV–VI.
  • Persistent/recurrent disease occurred in 7% of cancers (median 2.5 years), but 50% with concurrent high-risk mutations versus 0.8% (1/133) with isolated RAS. Only 11% (6/55) of non-resected nodules showed significant growth.
Clinical Relevance: Supports risk-stratified management of RAS-positive nodules, including lobectomy rather than total thyroidectomy for isolated RAS, and possibly surveillance in selected patients, which is relevant to UK practice, where molecular testing is not routine in most centres.
Limitations: Retrospective, single-centre design with short median follow-up (about 2.5 years) and selection bias in who underwent surgery, limiting conclusions on non-operative management.

Diabetologia

Gout as a risk factor for lower-extremity amputation in diabetes: a nationwide, register-based case-control study

Røikjer J, Kvist AV, Leutscher PDC et al. · 2026 Nov 03
Study Type: Nationwide register-based case-control study
Key Question: Is co-existing gout an independent risk factor for lower-extremity amputation (LEA) in people with type 2 diabetes?
Key Findings:
  • Gout was associated with higher LEA risk: unadjusted OR 1.85 (95% CI 1.69–2.02); fully adjusted OR 1.53 (1.37–1.69), after adjusting for diabetes duration, PAD, MI and late complications.
  • A significant trend across amputation levels (p=0.03) showed higher odds distally (toe OR 1.65, 1.32–2.05; above-knee OR 1.37, 1.12–1.68), but individual levels did not differ significantly.
  • Based on 4912 LEA cases and 39,101 age- and sex-matched controls drawn from 601,541 people with type 2 diabetes.
Clinical Relevance: Gout should be considered when assessing amputation risk in diabetic foot review, and may warrant closer foot surveillance and optimised urate management in UK diabetes and podiatry pathways.
Limitations: Observational register design means residual confounding and causality cannot be excluded, and gout was defined by coding and urate-lowering therapy rather than clinical verification, risking misclassification.

Diabetes Care

Common Genetic Variants Near SLC2A2 and Glycemic Response to Glimepiride in the GRADE Comparative Effectiveness Clinical Trial

Li JH, Szczerbinski L, Tripputi M et al. · 2026 Nov 05
Study Type: Pharmacogenomic GWAS nested within an RCT (GRADE), with replication cohorts, physiological studies and zebrafish functional validation.
Key Question: Do common genetic variants predict time to metabolic failure on glimepiride, glargine, liraglutide or sitagliptin added to metformin in type 2 diabetes?
Key Findings:
  • SLC2A2 (GLUT2) variant rs2129019, enriched in African/African American participants, conferred a 38% higher risk of metabolic failure per A allele on glimepiride (P = 1.55 × 10⁻⁸).
  • Carriers showed lower C-peptide index on OGTT and a blunted glucose-lowering response to acute sulfonylurea challenge, suggesting impaired β-cell function.
  • slc2a2-disrupted zebrafish had an attenuated response to glimepiride.
Clinical Relevance: Early evidence for genotype-guided sulfonylurea selection, particularly relevant for ethnically diverse UK populations, though not yet actionable in NHS practice.
Limitations: The abstract gives no replication results or findings for the other three drugs, and the effect is specific to one variant; clinical utility of genotype-guided prescribing remains untested.

Diabetologia

Genetic subtyping of MASLD reveals a glucose-lowering axis linked to GCKR alternative splicing

Wu F, Du M, Sun D et al. · 2026 Nov 03
Study Type: Genetic association study with functional validation (UK Biobank discovery, Taizhou Longitudinal Study replication, in vitro assays, in silico modelling)
Key Question: Does MASLD comprise genetically distinct subtypes with divergent glycaemic consequences, and what is the genetic basis of a glucose-lowering subtype?
Key Findings:
  • Partitioned polygenic risk scores split 18 MASLD variants into opposing axes: one lowered fasting glucose and type 2 diabetes risk, the others raised both. All axes were associated with higher liver injury markers and adverse liver outcomes. Glycaemic divergence replicated in the Taizhou cohort. (Effect sizes not given in the abstract.)
  • GCKR rs1260326 was prioritised as the lead shared MASLD-T2D signal and cis-pQTL for glucokinase regulatory protein (GKRP).
  • The T allele promoted exon-15 skipping, reducing full-length GKRP and producing a truncated isoform. Modelling suggests reduced glucokinase binding, which remains unvalidated experimentally.
Clinical Relevance: Supports MASLD heterogeneity and may eventually inform genetically guided risk stratification, but has no current role in NHS practice.
Limitations: The proposed mechanism rests partly on in silico prediction, and the findings are genetic and population-level rather than clinical, with no evidence yet of utility for individual patient management.

Diabetes Care

Longitudinal Changes in Exocrine Biomarkers in Children at Risk of Type 1 Diabetes in the ENDIA Study

Hall M, Penno MAS, Spelman T et al. · 2026 Nov 02
Study Type: Prospective birth cohort (ENDIA) with nested case-control analysis; adjusted linear mixed models.
Key Question: Do exocrine pancreatic biomarkers (faecal elastase-1 and serum immunoreactive trypsin) change early in the natural history of type 1 diabetes in at-risk children?
Key Findings:
  • FE-1 was lower in the first 6 months of life in children who later developed multiple islet autoantibodies or T1D (β at birth -0.61, 95% CI -1.04 to -0.17; at 3 months -0.39, 95% CI -0.69 to -0.09), consistent with delayed postnatal FE-1 rise.
  • IRT was lower in those who developed T1D at 12 months (β -0.30, 95% CI -0.58 to -0.02) and 18 months (β -0.40, 95% CI -0.71 to -0.10) before diagnosis, following islet autoantibody seroconversion.
  • Analysis drew on 1,679 stool samples (216 children) and 1,014 serum samples (242 children) from 301 at-risk children.
Clinical Relevance: Supports exocrine involvement in T1D pathogenesis and suggests non-invasive markers that could eventually refine risk stratification alongside UK islet autoantibody screening initiatives, though no clinical application yet.
Limitations: Abstract does not report absolute biomarker values, case numbers or predictive performance, so clinical utility cannot be judged.

Diabetologia

Associations of long-term exposure to air pollution with glucose homeostasis biomarkers and diabetes-related comorbidities in people with recent-onset type 1 and type 2 diabetes

Singh NM, Wigmann C, Kress S et al. · 2026 Nov 05
Study Type: Cross-sectional analysis of a prospective cohort (German Diabetes Study; n=1,120: 417 type 1, 703 type 2), with clamp-based phenotyping.
Key Question: Is long-term residential air pollution exposure associated with glucose homeostasis markers and diabetes-related comorbidities in recent-onset type 1 and type 2 diabetes?
Key Findings:
  • Type 2 diabetes: per IQR increase in PM2.5, higher HbA1c (exp[β] 1.04, 95% CI 1.01–1.06), lower insulin sensitivity (β −0.42, −0.82 to −0.03), lower insulin clearance, higher albuminuria (exp[β] 1.71, 1.41–2.08), lower VO2max, and higher odds of DSPN (OR 1.53, 1.02–2.32). CVD risk association was non-significant (CI crossed 1).
  • Type 1 diabetes: PM2.5 associated with higher HbA1c (1.07, 1.03–1.11), higher albuminuria (1.72, 1.34–2.20) and lower VO2max; findings were less consistent overall. PM10 and NO2 gave similar results.
  • Associations attenuated in two-pollutant models but persisted in cumulative risk index analyses.
Clinical Relevance: Supports air quality as a modifiable environmental contributor to glycaemic control and microvascular risk, relevant to UK urban populations and environmental health policy.
Limitations: Cross-sectional design precludes causal inference, and exposure was estimated at residential address only, so exposure misclassification and residual confounding are likely.

Diabetologia

Real-world evidence for decisions in diabetes

Misra S, Cigler M, El-Hakouni O et al. · 2026 Nov 05
Study Type: Narrative review/programme summary (REDDIE), incorporating registry analyses and target trial emulations; abstract does not specify methods in detail.
Key Question: Can real-world data generate credible, decision-relevant evidence in diabetes to complement randomised controlled trials?
Key Findings:
  • Well-designed observational analyses, including target trial emulations of landmark trials, can replicate major RCT findings and extend evidence to broader, under-represented populations and longer follow-up.
  • Credibility depends on alignment between research question, database fitness, study design and analytical methods.
  • Causal inference methods mitigate some biases but cannot resolve unmeasured confounding or incomplete variable capture in routine data.
  • No quantitative effect sizes or replication metrics are reported in the abstract.
Clinical Relevance: Provides a framework for appraising RWE in diabetes, relevant to UK clinicians interpreting registry-based studies and to NICE/MHRA use of real-world evidence in decision-making.
Limitations: Abstract provides no quantitative data on how closely emulations replicated trial results, so the strength of the replication claim cannot be assessed.
